title: Life-sustaining autologous solid organs assembled for implantation

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a surgically implantable solid organ or organ segment built with the recipient’s own cells that performs enough organ-specific work to sustain life. Examples include a kidney that supplies adequate renal function, a hepatic lobe that supplies adequate liver function, or a heart that sustains circulation. The construct would need blood vessels that a surgeon can connect to the recipient’s circulation and an internal vascular network that supports its living tissue. These are proposed capabilities, not achievements established by the supplied evidence.

One engineering route uses a decellularized organ scaffold: cellular material is removed from an existing organ, and the remaining structure is repopulated with cells. The supplied review of the June 2025 Nature Reviews Bioengineering preview confirms that this approach can use autologous or allogeneic cells. SUR-12 specifically concerns autologous cellular composition. Printing and other assembly methods remain possible routes within the concept, but no particular manufacturing method defines its completion.

Scope definition: the decisive endpoint is life-sustaining function after implantation. A structural replacement, a cardiac patch that assists an existing heart, or an isolated construct producing urine or albumin on a laboratory pump would not by itself meet that endpoint. Manufacturing could take place before a planned operation, with time for maturation. Assembly during the same anesthetic, especially from a fresh biopsy, would be an additional manufacturing achievement rather than a prerequisite for this concept.

significance.text: The June 2025 organ-engineering review describes a shortage in which patients awaiting donor organs outnumber available organs. If autologous engineered organs could reliably provide life-sustaining function, a recipient could receive replacement function without a donated human organ. That would create a major new source of transplantable organs. A single successful implant would establish an important capability, while dependable clinical supply would additionally require reproducible production, acceptable manufacturing times and consistent outcomes.

Autologous cells offer a plausible immunologic advantage by avoiding donor-cell alloreactivity. The reviewed preview presents reduced rejection risk and less need for lifelong immunosuppression as potential benefits of bioengineered organs; it does not demonstrate that immunosuppression can be eliminated. The complete construct would still require evaluation, including its scaffold and interactions with the recipient. Patient-derived cells therefore do not automatically establish immune compatibility of the entire implant.

Conditional implications: planned implantation after weeks of maturation could change organ supply even without same-day manufacture. Wider availability would depend on whether production can serve many patients rather than a few exceptional cases. Lifelong durability, growth with a pediatric recipient, and extension from one organ to another would each require additional evidence. Innervation requirements would depend on the organ and the function being claimed; they should not be treated as identical for kidneys, liver tissue and hearts.

missing_breakthrough.text: The best-supported technical barrier in the supplied evidence is functional vascularization. The June 20, 2025 Nature Biomedical Engineering review identifies inadequate vasculature as a constraint on engineered-tissue survival and describes the need to guide vascular formation across micrometre-to-millimetre scales. The engineering challenge is therefore not simply adding a large inlet and outlet: blood delivery must reach the living tissue throughout the construct.

Engineering requirements inferred from the proposed endpoint include vessels that remain patent after surgical connection, sufficiently mature and coordinated organ-specific cells, adequate mechanical integrity, and enough functioning tissue to support the recipient. Scaling from small tissue constructs to an implant with clinically adequate capacity must preserve both perfusion and function. The supplied previews do not establish the relative importance of these barriers or document the extent to which each has already been overcome; they remain requirements to demonstrate rather than a verified ranking of present bottlenecks.

The decellularized-scaffold review describes recellularization, modifications intended to support engraftment and function, and interactions between the transplant and recipient. Its preview supports treating successful implantation as an integration problem involving the whole construct. Autologous cellular origin addresses one source of immune mismatch, while scaffold compatibility and other recipient responses still require evaluation. The supplied evidence does not justify the earlier assertion that immunologic rejection is necessarily secondary in every autologous construct.

Manufacturing synthesis: a clinically useful process would also have to produce sufficiently consistent constructs, establish their readiness for implantation and fit the patient’s treatment timeline. Same-session assembly from a fresh biopsy would impose a substantially tighter production and maturation constraint. Solving that harder timing problem is separable from demonstrating a life-sustaining organ manufactured in advance.

current_state.text: The supplied review confirms the identity and abstract content of Strategies for the vascular patterning of engineered tissues for organ repair, published June 20, 2025. Its abstract supports the vascularization barrier and the micrometre-to-millimetre patterning requirement. The retained material was a subscription preview; the review body and figures were not inspected. This source supplies a dated account of an engineering challenge, not a demonstrated life-sustaining autologous organ implant.

The supplied review also confirms the preview of Ex vivo organ engineering using decellularized tissue scaffolds, published June 16, 2025. It describes scaffolds repopulated with autologous or allogeneic cells, intended engraftment and function after transplantation, and challenges in clinical translation. Only the preview was substantively reviewed. It establishes the engineering approach and its translational aims, but does not establish a quantitative level of achieved organ function or successful life support in a recipient.

The reconciled research attributes basic liver or kidney function in recellularized tissues to a Lancet review reported as published July 26, 2025. However, no copy of that source was captured for the validated review. The attribution therefore remains unverified within this evidence set and cannot serve here as a confirmed demonstration of functional performance. The missing source is a limitation of the available evidence, not evidence that the reported tissue functions are false.

The research likewise attributes prolonged survival and bridging to liver transplantation to a Hepatology review, with an April 3, 2025 electronic publication date and a 2026 journal citation. The retained PubMed copy contains only a cookie-access message, so the validated review could not verify the article identity, dates or attributed abstract from that copy. The claims about liver-cell therapy, organoids and bioprinted hepatic tissue remain unverified here. Conceptually, evidence of bridging treatment or sophisticated tissue function would still need to be distinguished from an implantable organ that independently supplies life-sustaining replacement function.

No substantive passage identified in the supplied review reports a human life-sustaining autologous solid-organ implant or same-session assembly meeting this concept’s scope. The limited previews cannot establish that no such result exists. Although the source copies were retrieved on November 1, 2026, the supplied freshness record is empty, so retrieval does not establish coverage of developments after the June 2025 reviews. No verified quantitative filtration or survival result meeting the proposed endpoint is available in this evidence set.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed initial demonstration: in a large animal, an autologous kidney or hepatic lobe connected through a surgical vascular anastomosis sustains the recipient for at least 30 days after removal or functional exclusion of native organ support. Organ-specific function should fall within a prespecified range against an appropriate conventional graft comparator. Thirty days is a proposed early milestone, not an established consensus threshold or evidence of lifelong replacement.
completion_criteria.label: Autologous kidney or hepatic lobe sustains 30-day large-animal survival

completion_criteria.text: Proposed attribution requirements: the protocol should establish that survival and relevant function depend on the construct rather than residual native function or unreported replacement treatment. Dialysis, mechanical circulatory support and other organ-replacement interventions should be explicitly documented, with permitted support and failure criteria defined in advance. Measurements should assess adequate integrated organ function; urine production or albumin secretion alone would not establish completion.
completion_criteria.label: Survival and integrated organ function demonstrably depend on the construct

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: a first human series would need dialysis-free or liver-failure-free survival, as appropriate, over a prespecified interval without a donor organ. A cardiac replacement would require a separate demonstration that the implant sustains circulation; a kidney or liver result would not establish that capability. A cardiac patch that does not sustain circulation would remain outside the replacement endpoint.
completion_criteria.label: Human implants sustain dialysis-free or liver-failure-free survival without donor organs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: convincing evidence should include repeated success across independently manufactured constructs and recipients, sufficiently described methods for independent replication, and follow-up addressing sustained function and construct-related complications. Reports should state cell and scaffold origins, manufacturing and maturation times, whether assembly occurred during implantation, and the recipient conditions under which the result applies. Longer follow-up and broader testing would be needed for claims about durability, pediatric growth or additional organ types. Finite studies establish demonstrated breadth under tested conditions rather than universal suitability.
completion_criteria.label: Independently manufactured constructs repeatedly succeed with replication methods and limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: SUR-02, Destination-therapy solid-organ xenotransplantation, shares the goal of supplying life-sustaining replacement organs beyond the human-donor pool. Its distinguishing route is an organ from another species; SUR-12 instead concerns an engineered construct with autologous cells. Success in one would not establish the other’s manufacturing or recipient-compatibility requirements.

Roster-based comparison: SUR-09, Living, perfused autologous replacements for complex parts that grafts do not supply, overlaps strongly in fabrication, living tissue and perfusion. SUR-12 has the additional defining endpoint of life-sustaining solid-organ parenchymal function. Decellularized scaffolds can contribute evidence or methods to both concepts without becoming a separate innovation entry or making the endpoints interchangeable.

Roster-based comparison: SUR-01, Operational donor-specific tolerance for the transplants patients actually receive, concerns recipient acceptance of donor tissue. SUR-12 seeks an autologous cellular composition, which may reduce donor-cell alloreactivity but does not itself prove complete immune compatibility or freedom from immunosuppression. Tolerance and organ fabrication remain distinct capabilities.

Roster-based comparison: SUR-03, Life-sustaining cryobanking of human-scale organs, concerns preservation and storage rather than creating replacement organs. It could become complementary if engineered organs could also be banked, but SUR-12 does not require cryobanking. SUR-05, Adult surgical wounds that heal by regeneration rather than fibrosis, shares a regenerative ambition while addressing healing within the patient; SUR-12 concerns an assembled implant that supplies replacement organ function.

change_log.change: Preserved SUR-12 and its title while clarifying that life-sustaining function after implantation defines the concept.
change_log.reason: This retains the candidate’s identity and distinguishes the endpoint from structural repair, supportive patches and isolated laboratory outputs.

change_log.change: Integrated scaffold recellularization, autologous cellular composition and the distinction between advance maturation and same-session assembly.
change_log.reason: These details explain both the engineering route and why planned manufacture could change organ supply without same-day production.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical claims of present-day nonachievement with a bounded description of what the supplied evidence reports.
change_log.reason: Partial June 2025 previews and an empty freshness record cannot establish comprehensive absence through November 2026.

change_log.change: Retained vascularization as the documented barrier and recast patency, maturity, mechanical integrity and implant-scale capacity as endpoint-derived engineering requirements.
change_log.reason: The supplied review directly supports vascularization but does not establish the full barrier list or rank its components.

change_log.change: Qualified the immunologic benefit and removed the assertion that autologous origin guarantees freedom from graft-related immunosuppression.
change_log.reason: Avoiding donor-cell alloreactivity does not establish compatibility of the complete construct, including its scaffold.

change_log.change: Preserved the Lancet basic-function and Hepatology bridging claims as explicitly unverified attributions.
change_log.reason: No Lancet artifact was captured, and the PubMed copy contains only an access message; these limitations neither confirm nor refute the underlying claims.

change_log.change: Excluded the unrelated FDA hernia-graft PDF and the untraced Cureus primate-filtration narrative from substantive evidence.
change_log.reason: Neither supplies reviewed evidence of the proposed life-sustaining engineered solid-organ capability.

change_log.change: Strengthened the proposed completion framework with dependence on the construct, organ-appropriate comparators, support disclosure and a separate cardiac endpoint.
change_log.reason: These distinctions prevent residual native function, replacement treatment or success in another organ from being mistaken for completion.

change_log.change: Added reproducibility, manufacturing boundaries and explicit limits on what finite demonstrations establish.
change_log.reason: An early survival milestone does not establish dependable clinical supply, lifelong durability or applicability across organs and recipients.

change_log.change: Used the supplied roster to explain related concepts without merging entries.
change_log.reason: The roster supports bounded conceptual comparisons, including SUR-02 and SUR-09, while preserving each concept’s distinct endpoint.

unresolved_issues: The field’s state through November 2026 remains unresolved because the supplied freshness record contains no search evidence establishing coverage after the dated reviews.
The Lancet basic-function attribution needs a substantive source copy or traceable primary studies before the demonstrated functions, species, scale and duration can be specified.
The Hepatology article identity, publication details and attributed liver-bridging findings could not be verified from the retained cookie-access message.
The supplied previews do not establish achieved post-anastomosis patency, mechanical competence, parenchymal maturity or their relative importance across kidney, liver and heart constructs.
Whether a complete autologous construct can avoid immunosuppression remains dependent on its cellular composition, scaffold and recipient responses.
The proposed 30-day milestone, comparator ranges, permitted supportive treatments and human follow-up interval require organ-specific protocol choices; no consensus standard is established here.
No traceable primary evidence was supplied for the excluded Cureus primate-filtration claim, so its quantitative performance remains unresolved.
Reliable production, long-term durability, pediatric growth and extension to additional organ types remain separate questions beyond an initial successful implant.

brief.title: Life-saving replacement organs made from your own cells
possible: A person with organ failure could receive a replacement made with their own cells, without waiting for a donated human organ. An implanted kidney, liver section or heart would do enough work to keep them alive.

Surgeons could connect its blood vessels to the patient’s circulation. Smaller vessels inside would keep the tissue supplied with blood. The organ could be grown and matured before a planned operation.
why: More people need transplants than there are donor organs. Reliable production of replacement organs could create another source for patients who need them.
Using a patient’s own cells could reduce immune rejection and the need for lifelong drugs that suppress the immune system.

sources.who: Tarek Saleh, Lorenzo Caciolli, Giovanni Giuseppe Giobbe and colleagues
sources.showed: Their review describes removing cells from organs to leave a supporting scaffold, then adding new cells. Large-animal organs can provide structures large enough for human-sized replacements.
sources.quote: Organs of large animals can be decellularized to create scaffolds for the engineering of human-sized organs.
sources.cited_for: It supports rebuilding organs around an existing tissue structure using the recipient’s own cells.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate an implanted organ made with the recipient’s cells that supplies life-sustaining function.

sources.who: Authors of the review on transplantable organs
sources.showed: This review covers advances in transplantable organs, including basic liver or kidney function in tissues repopulated with cells.
sources.cited_for: It concerns early organ function in rebuilt tissues.
sources.not_established: Basic tissue function does not establish that an implanted organ can keep a recipient alive.

sources.who: Kevin D. Janson, Siavash Parkhideh and colleagues
sources.showed: Their review identifies a working blood-vessel network as a barrier to engineered tissue survival. It describes the need to guide vessel formation from tiny vessels to larger ones.
sources.quote: However, the survival of engineered tissues is constrained by the challenge of establishing a functional vasculature.
sources.cited_for: It explains why blood must reach tissue throughout an engineered organ.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate a vessel network that supports life-sustaining replacement function after implantation.

sources.who: Shaoyang Qin, Xiaochen Bo, Hongyuan Liu, Zhishuo Zhang, Zhicong Zhao and Qiang Xia
sources.showed: Their review reports that cell transplants have prolonged patient survival while awaiting liver transplantation. It also describes lab-grown liver tissues with complex structures and functions.
sources.quote: Several clinical studies have demonstrated that stem cell transplantation and hepatocyte transplantation can prolong patient survival and serve as a bridge to liver transplantation.
sources.cited_for: It supports progress in liver cell treatments and tissue engineering.
sources.not_established: Helping patients survive until transplantation does not establish an independently life-sustaining replacement organ made from their own cells.

shown: Qin and colleagues report that cell transplants have helped patients survive until liver transplantation. They also describe lab-grown liver tissues with complex structures and functions. These are steps toward replacement function, but do not demonstrate an implanted organ made from the recipient’s cells that independently sustains life.
missing: An implanted organ must deliver enough coordinated function to sustain life without help from the failing native organ.
Its blood vessels must stay open after surgical connection and supply living tissue throughout the organ.
The whole implant, including its supporting structure, must work safely with the recipient’s body.
Production must repeatedly deliver organs ready for implantation within patients’ treatment timelines.

milestones.label: A kidney or liver section sustains large-animal survival
milestones.explanation: A kidney or liver section made with the animal’s own cells would have to sustain life for 30 days without native organ support, with function in a preset range against a conventional transplant. This would establish early replacement capacity.

milestones.label: Survival demonstrably depends on the implanted organ
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to establish that survival and adequate organ function depend on the implant, with other replacement treatments documented and limits set beforehand. This would distinguish replacement from partial assistance.

milestones.label: Human recipients survive without a donor organ
milestones.explanation: A human series would have to show survival without dialysis, a blood-filtering treatment, or liver failure for a preset period without donor organs. This would establish human replacement; a heart would need separate proof of circulation.

milestones.label: Separately manufactured organs repeatedly succeed
milestones.explanation: Repeated implants would have to sustain function, with complications tracked and methods, cell and scaffold origins, production timing and recipient conditions described. This would establish repeatability and the limits of demonstrated use.

uncertain: Whether an entire implant made with the patient’s cells can avoid immune-suppressing drugs remains unresolved.
The proposed 30-day test and acceptable function, support and human follow-up periods need organ-specific choices.
Long-term durability, growth with children and success across different organ types remain separate questions.

page.title: Life-sustaining autologous tissue-engineered solid organs
page.definition: An implanted solid organ or organ segment takes over enough of a failing organ’s work to sustain the recipient’s life. Surgically connected vessels supply blood through the graft’s internal vascular network. Autologous means the living cells used to build the graft come from the recipient. Its supporting scaffold can come from a donor organ whose cells have been removed. A related clinical implant has added donor-derived muscle to a patient’s failing heart, which continued to provide the pump.

goal.need: On 30 July 2026, 95,492 people were waiting for a kidney in the U.S., 8,776 for a liver and 4,039 for a heart. Some patients wait years for a compatible donor organ, and some die waiting. A graft grown in time from a patient’s own cells could shorten that wait and, if immune compatible, spare the recipient lifelong anti-rejection drugs. For patients with an inherited disorder, the cells used to make the graft may carry the same defect.

figures.caption: U.S. organ waiting lists and single-organ transplantation

completion.title: An implanted autologous engineered organ supplies life-sustaining function in a human.
completion.criterion: A peer-reviewed clinical report demonstrates that an implanted, surgically vascularized solid organ or segment made with its recipient’s own cells supplies the function necessary to keep that recipient alive throughout the study’s prespecified observation period. Native organ function is absent or insufficient, and no donor graft or other replacement of the claimed function supplies that life support. The evidence establishes dependence on the construct. Success applies to the organ tested; no numerical minimum follow-up is asserted.
completion.set_by: Atlas provisional capability test; no published human completion threshold specific to autologous engineered solid organs was located.
completion.basis: Searched PRINT’s solicitation, Health Canada’s cell-therapy guidance and ClinicalTrials.gov for a human autologous solid-organ life-support endpoint; found animal targets and general clinical stages, but no completion threshold. This provisional test follows the stated organ-replacement goal without assigning an unsupported survival duration. The scaffold and vascularization reviews support the construct’s scope, rather than a clinical success threshold.

milestones.title: A perfused tissue-engineered organ exhibits an organ-specific function.
milestones.criterion: Measure organ-specific work in a tissue-engineered construct during laboratory perfusion. For a heart, demonstrate pumping under load. For a liver, demonstrate synthesis of a liver product such as albumin or urea. For a kidney, demonstrate filtration across the glomerular barrier.
milestones.set_by: Whole-organ bioengineering convention demonstrated by the functional assays of Ott and colleagues, Uygun and colleagues, and Lo and colleagues. The quoted requirement concerns the heart.
milestones.threshold_quote: Generating a bioartificial heart requires engineering of cardiac architecture, appropriate cellular constituents and pump function.

milestones.title: Bioprinted organs remain viable for 3–6 months in more than ten small animals.
milestones.criterion: Successfully implant bioprinted organs in more than 10 small animals and demonstrate graft viability for 3–6 months. Assess organ function in humanized mice. Demonstrate absence of teratomas, rejection, toxicity and mutagenicity, and verify normal organ structure and host response after death. PRINT permits recipient-derived or immune-compatible donor cells.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-H PRINT, Table 2, M3.6 and the Phase I deliverable for organ function in humanized mice.
milestones.threshold_quote:
in >10 small animals.
Demonstrate viability and longevity of the bioprinted
organ in small animal model (3–6-month survival).

milestones.title: Bioprinted organs remain viable for 3–6 months in more than five large animals.
milestones.criterion: Implant bioprinted organs in more than five large animals. Demonstrate viability for 3–6 months, normal graft function in humanized pigs with severe combined immunodeficiency, and absence of teratomas, rejection and toxicity at six months. Kidney examples are filtration of 100–200 mL/min/70 kg, renal blood flow of 3–5 mL/min/g and serum creatinine <2 mg/dL. Heart examples are 60–120 beats/min, output of 3–6 L/min and ejection fraction of 50–70%. Liver examples are ALT 30–60, AST 30–85 and ALP 40–180 U/L, serum creatinine <2 mg/dL and bilirubin ≤1 mg/dL. Examine organ structure after death by immunohistochemistry and molecular markers.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-H PRINT, amended solicitation, Table 2, M3.10 and the Phase II deliverable. The functional ranges are programme examples.
milestones.threshold_quote: humanized SCID pig model and survival of 3-6 months post transplantation

milestones.title: An autologous engineered organ is implanted in an authorised first-in-human safety trial.
milestones.criterion: In an authorised first-in-human trial with product safety as a primary endpoint, implant an engineered solid organ or organ segment made with the living participant’s own cells and surgically connect the graft to that participant’s circulation.
milestones.set_by: Health Canada, cell-therapy guidance, sections 2.2.1 and 2.4.3.2; a general first-in-human development stage, not an organ-specific protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: Early trials will include first in human trials and dose determination / tolerance studies with primary endpoints focussed on product safety.

milestones.title: A bioprinted organ meets PRINT’s organ-specific functional targets under laboratory perfusion.
milestones.criterion: Measure function during in vitro perfusion of the bioprinted organ. PRINT’s kidney examples are renal blood flow of 100–350 and glomerular filtration rate of 15–80, both in “ml/min*100 g” as printed. Heart examples are 60–120 beats/min, cardiac output of 3–6 L/min and ejection fraction of 50–70%. Liver examples are oxygen consumption of 1–5 mL O₂/min/100 g and alanine and aspartate aminotransferase activities each below 2,000 U/L. PRINT permits teams to propose justified alternative metrics.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-H PRINT, amended solicitation, Table 2, M3.5 and section 1.3.

not_found: No registered protocol specifying independent life support by an implanted autologous engineered kidney, liver or heart was located.
The supplied Lancet review and substantive text of the supplied Hepatology review could not be opened.
The publisher’s October 2026 miroliverELAP conference abstract could not be opened.
No programme or professional-society statement was found judging autologous solid-organ replacement infeasible or unworthy of pursuit.

results.finding: Engineered rat hearts (n=8 maintained under perfusion) pumped under load at about 2% of adult heart function.
results.detail: The excerpt gives the number of constructs maintained under perfusion. The number that underwent the working-heart pump test is unspecified.
results.quote: By day 8, under physiological load and electrical stimulation, constructs could generate pump function (equivalent to about 2% of adult or 25% of 16-week fetal heart function) in a modified working heart preparation.

results.finding: Recellularized porcine liver grafts showed increasing albumin and urea production during a 4-day perfusion interval. Assay n unspecified.
results.quote: In pretransplant of the graft, ALB production, urea secretion, and production of coagulation factors gradually improved.

results.finding: Recellularized porcine liver grafts showed increasing synthesis of liver products during a 4-day perfusion interval. Assay n unspecified.
results.quote: In pretransplant of the graft, ALB production, urea secretion, and production of coagulation factors gradually improved.

results.finding: Engineered liver grafts retained metabolic activity through day 28 in a study with 7 porcine recipients.
results.detail: Five recipients remained after two surgical deaths. The residual native liver could have contributed to the blood test results, and portal-vein anastomotic stenosis limited graft perfusion.
results.quote: These analyses showed that the graft maintained its hepatic metabolic activity until POD 28

results.finding: Five bioengineered kidneys with podocytes showed glomerular filtration throughout 60 minutes of laboratory perfusion.
results.quote: In comparison, bi-culture BEKs with recellularized glomeruli demonstrated urine with significantly lower protein and hematocrit values relative to serum throughout the 1-hour perfusion period, indicating filtration capabilities.

results.finding: Laboratory perfusion of bioengineered kidneys (five per group) used blood flow of 300–800 mL/min.
results.detail: The reported flow lacks the per-100 g normalization required for direct comparison with PRINT’s example. Protein and red blood cell exclusion indicate filtration selectivity.
results.quote: The resulting perfusion flow rates were between 300 mL/min and 800 mL/min.

results.finding: Five bioengineered kidney grafts were tested in pigs. The final graft showed filtration for up to 5 hours.
results.detail: Filtration in the final session was assessed by urine protein and hematocrit. The study did not establish normal glomerular filtration rate, mass-normalized renal blood flow, or serum creatinine.
results.quote: While implant 3 only tested a single BEK, this implant extended the examination window up to 5 hours, demonstrating sustained filtration function with remarkably low (around 1%) urine hematocrit and lower urine protein levels compared to serum protein levels (Fig.

results.finding: Bioprinted human liver tissue stained positive for human albumin after 21 days in vitro (sample size unspecified).
results.detail: The in vitro assay localized albumin in the tissue. The circulating albumin assay was performed after implantation.
results.quote: BTLT stained for hAlbumin (red) and hCD31 (green) after 3 (c) or 21 (d) days reveal the presence of densely arranged human hepatocytes which are supported by organized networks of microvascular structures.

results.finding: Bioprinted human liver grafts in PiZ mice had mature perfused vasculature at 90 days (sample size unspecified).
results.quote:
The presence of mature, perfused vasculature in the BTLT at 90 days post-implantation
confirms robust engraftment and cellular retention, a key limitation to most traditional cell
therapy approaches.

results.finding: In a 32-rat implantation study, viable human kidney cells persisted in bioprinted renal defect constructs for up to 2 months.
results.detail: The total of 32 rats includes all four groups, including acellular and GelMA controls. The authors assessed cell persistence and tissue formation by histology and immunofluorescence. Renal function was unmeasured.
results.quote: immunofluorescent analyses employing human‐specific markers confirmed the presence of viable human cells within the bioprinted constructs up to 2 months post‐implantation.

results.finding: Bioprinted human liver organoids secreted more albumin and produced more urea nitrogen than 2D hepatocyte cultures (n = 3 per group).
results.detail: The text reports the direction and significance of the differences. Figure 3F contains the concentration data.
results.quote: Compared to 2D-cultured hiHeps, 3DP-HHO exhibited significantly higher levels of urea nitrogen production and albumin secretion, two key indicators of liver-specific metabolic and synthetic function ( Fig. 3 F).

results.finding: Mice with bioprinted liver organoid grafts (n = 5) had detectable human albumin in serum two weeks after implantation.
results.detail: Other mouse experiments used separate injury models and dose groups. They did not establish a cohort of more than 10 recipients with viable grafts at 3–6 months.
results.quote: Notably, two weeks post-implantation, human albumin was detectable in the serum of treated mice, with significantly higher levels observed in the 3DP-HHO group compared to hiHeps and GelMA controls ( Fig. 4 I).

results.finding: Bama minipigs implanted with bioprinted liver organoids (n = 5, 4 controls) had a median survival of 120 hours.
results.detail: The discs were affixed to the liver remnant. Human albumin was initially detectable, but serum albumin remained below normal and declined. The reported three-month observations concern host outcomes.
results.quote: a significant extension of median survival from 30 h to 120 h

results.finding: Human nephron sheets in NSG mice (six implantations) showed size-selective filtration of 3 kDa dextran.
results.detail: The in vitro dextran assay added tracer to the culture medium and assessed diffusion and uptake. It did not perfuse the glomerular vessels.
results.quote: Intravital imaging of a nephron sheet implanted in a dorsal skinfold chamber of mice revealed filtration function with size selectability in the organoid glomeruli vascularized with human endothelia.

results.finding: Human nephron sheets in NSG mice (six implantations) showed filtration during follow-up through day 11.
results.detail: The paper identifies the hosts as immunodeficient NSG mice. It does not report humanization beyond implantation of the human tissue being tested.
results.quote: Multiphoton intravital microscopy (MP-IVM) was performed between days 6 and 11 following the implantation of nephron sheets to evaluate their potential filtration function.

results.finding: Of 32 bioprinted Fontan conduits implanted in mice, Moderate and Soft grafts showed synchronous contractions at 6 months.
results.detail: The sample size counts implanted conduits. The abstract gives neither a separate mouse count nor the number of grafts assessed for contractile function at 6 months.
results.quote: Moderate and Soft grafts demonstrated robust, synchronous contractions and generated mean systolic pressures of 4.7 mmHg and 8.4 mmHg at 6 months, respectively, compared to <1 mmHg in Stiff grafts.

results.finding: Engineered heart muscle loops from 18 implantation batches underwent contractility testing with 1.5 Hz stimulation.
results.detail: Stretching the loops provided preload for measuring twitch force. The assay measured force without fluid ejection.
results.quote:
Contractile function measured under isometric 
conditions and electrical field stimulation at 1.5 Hz

results.finding: Viable rhesus engineered heart muscle was detectable in nude rats (n=7 viable-graft recipients) at 4 weeks.
results.detail: The feasibility study used rhesus-to-rat xenografts. The separate six-month observation addresses ectopic cartilage and bone, with no six-month viability or functional result stated.
results.quote:
rhesus macaque CMs could be identified 4 weeks after implantation of 
viable but not lethally irradiated EHM (Extended Data Fig. 2b).

results.finding: Engineered heart muscle allografts in rhesus macaques (n=3 in the healthy tacrolimus-plus-methylprednisolone group) retained cardiomyocytes at 6 months.
results.detail: Follow-up counts include animals with rejection. Ejection fraction describes the recipient heart. The study also reported immunosuppressant-related adverse effects.
results.quote:
CM allografts 
were retained under tacrolimus and methylprednisolone for 6 months 
(Fig. 2).

results.finding: Epicardial engineered heart muscle allografts remained visible at heart explant in a BioVAT-HF patient (n=1) after 3 months.
results.detail: The patient’s native heart continued pumping during follow-up. Histological capillaries establish vascularization of the patch, while the reported procedure was epicardial placement.
results.quote:
Explanted heart obtained 
3 months after EHM implantation from a successfully heart transplanted 
BioVAT-HF patient (ID: 27016). EHMs were macroscopically visible as epicardial 
grafts (encircled) and are marked with asterisks in the cross-section (right).

results.finding: Recellularized rat kidneys (sample size unspecified) achieved approximately 10% of cadaveric kidney creatinine clearance during laboratory perfusion.
results.detail: The study estimated glomerular filtration from whole-organ creatinine clearance and assessed barrier selectivity through albumin retention. The supplied text gives no group sample sizes for the perfusion assay.
results.quote: After repopulation with endothelial and epithelial cells, creatinine clearance of regenerated constructs reached approximately 10% of cadaveric kidneys, which indicates a decrease of glomerular filtration across a partially reconstituted and likely immature glomerular membrane

results.finding: Human liver cell–seeded bioengineered grafts (n = 8) yielded a mean urea concentration of 0.525 µM/L/million cells during laboratory perfusion.
results.detail: Urea was measured in conditioned culture medium collected after 24 hours of bioreactor perfusion. The separate whole-blood assay assessed vascular patency.
results.quote: BELs seeded with PHLCs demonstrated higher urea (0.525 ± 0.090 vs. 0.160 ± 0.025 µM/L/million cells;  p  < 0.0001)

results.finding: Engineered human ventricular microchambers (n = 4 devices) sustained unidirectional flow against an estimated mean afterload of 28.6 Pa.
results.detail: A glass column and flow constrictor imposed the afterload. The authors measured flow by particle image velocimetry and used finite-element models to estimate pressure.
results.quote:
Interestingly, the unidirectional flow was sustained despite the pres-
ence of the afterload in all tested devices, suggesting that the loaded 
miniPUMP exhibits a complete PV loop.

definition = "An implanted solid organ or organ segment takes over enough of a failing organ\u2019s work to sustain the recipient\u2019s life. Surgically connected vessels supply blood through the graft\u2019s internal vascular network. Autologous means the living cells used to build the graft come from the recipient. Its supporting scaffold can come from a donor organ whose cells have been removed. A related clinical implant has added donor-derived muscle to a patient\u2019s failing heart, which continued to provide the pump.". Reason: The definition leaves the scaffold’s origin unclear and gives no clinical example that distinguishes heart repair from replacement.

goal.need = "On 30 July 2026, 95,492 people were waiting for a kidney in the U.S., 8,776 for a liver and 4,039 for a heart. Some patients wait years for a compatible donor organ, and some die waiting. A graft grown in time from a patient\u2019s own cells could shorten that wait and, if immune compatible, spare the recipient lifelong anti-rejection drugs. For patients with an inherited disorder, the cells used to make the graft may carry the same defect.". Reason: The waiting-list figures establish the scale of need, but the comparison with annual transplant counts leaves out what a patient-derived graft could change for someone awaiting a donor.

add statement by University of California San Diego, ARPA-H-funded liver bioprinting project, 2026: "livers grown from a patient’s own cells.". Reason: The funded liver project explicitly specifies the patient’s own cells, while the broader PRINT goal also permits banked donor cells.

edit m1: criterion = "Measure organ-specific work in a tissue-engineered construct during laboratory perfusion. For a heart, demonstrate pumping under load. For a liver, demonstrate synthesis of a liver product such as albumin or urea. For a kidney, demonstrate filtration across the glomerular barrier."; refs = [8, 9, 10]. Reason: The criterion mixes the laboratory test with dated results from three studies.

add milestone after m1: "A bioprinted organ meets PRINT’s organ-specific functional targets under laboratory perfusion.". Reason: PRINT defines a quantitative perfusion assay between the first measurable organ function and implantation in small animals.

edit m2: criterion = "Successfully implant bioprinted organs in more than 10 small animals and demonstrate graft viability for 3\u20136 months. Assess organ function in humanized mice. Demonstrate absence of teratomas, rejection, toxicity and mutagenicity, and verify normal organ structure and host response after death. PRINT permits recipient-derived or immune-compatible donor cells."; set_by = "ARPA-H PRINT, Table 2, M3.6 and the Phase I deliverable for organ function in humanized mice."; threshold_quote = "in >10 small animals.\nDemonstrate viability and longevity of the bioprinted\norgan in small animal model (3\u20136-month survival)."; threshold_ref = 4; refs = [4, 22]. Reason: The small-animal target lacks its source quotation and omits PRINT’s specified functional assessment in humanized mice.

edit m3: criterion = "Implant bioprinted organs in more than five large animals. Demonstrate viability for 3\u20136 months, normal graft function in humanized pigs with severe combined immunodeficiency, and absence of teratomas, rejection and toxicity at six months. Kidney examples are filtration of 100\u2013200 mL/min/70 kg, renal blood flow of 3\u20135 mL/min/g and serum creatinine <2 mg/dL. Heart examples are 60\u2013120 beats/min, output of 3\u20136 L/min and ejection fraction of 50\u201370%. Liver examples are ALT 30\u201360, AST 30\u201385 and ALP 40\u2013180 U/L, serum creatinine <2 mg/dL and bilirubin \u22641 mg/dL. Examine organ structure after death by immunohistochemistry and molecular markers."; set_by = "ARPA-H PRINT, amended solicitation, Table 2, M3.10 and the Phase II deliverable. The functional ranges are programme examples."; threshold_quote = "humanized SCID pig model and survival of 3-6 months post transplantation"; threshold_ref = 22; refs = [22]. Reason: The criterion includes a pig-study result and omits the amended solicitation’s specified model for demonstrating normal organ function.

edit m4: criterion = "In an authorised first-in-human trial with product safety as a primary endpoint, implant an engineered solid organ or organ segment made with the living participant\u2019s own cells and surgically connect the graft to that participant\u2019s circulation."; refs = [5]. Reason: The first-in-human criterion includes reports about an external liver-support device that do not define the implantation test.
